didactic

/dy-DAK-tik/ - the stress falls on DAK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Didactic means intended to instruct, with a lecturing or moralizing tone.

The gardening column turned didactic this spring, capping each entry with a numbered lesson on discipline.

Example

Half the cookbook is recipes; the other half is small sermons. The pie chapter opens with two pages on thrift, and the bread section pauses to praise patience before the flour is measured. Reviewers call the book didactic — determined to improve the cook, not just feed one.

Didactic means built to instruct, and it usually carries a whiff of heavy-handedness: the lesson is pressed on you. It is narrower than pedagogical, which describes teaching methods neutrally, and stronger than informative — didactic work wants you improved, not merely informed.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

moralizing: Moralizing work pushes judgments of right and wrong at its audience — every scene closes on a verdict about how to live. Didactic is wider: a didactic book is built to instruct, and the lesson it presses may be moral, practical, or technical. All moralizing is pushy teaching; not all didactic teaching moralizes.

lecturing: Lecturing is instruction delivered at you whether or not you asked — the word catches a speaker's manner in the moment. Didactic describes design rather than delivery: a work is didactic because it was built to improve its audience, even when its tone stays gentle from page to page.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

open-ended: leaving the conclusions for the audience to draw

escapist: made to entertain, with no designs on improving anyone

Where it sits · how hard the lesson is pressed

informative → didactic → sermonizing

informative vs. didactic: Informative is milder than didactic — an informative piece hands you facts and lets you be; nothing is pressed.

sermonizing vs. didactic: Sermonizing goes further than didactic: didactic work at least means to teach, while sermonizing has given up teaching for pure moral scolding.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — didact-: to teach (Greek didaskein)

Suffix — -ic: adjective: of or like

Put it together: Didact- (to teach) + -ic = of teaching. Greek didaktikos described anything apt at teaching; English kept the teaching and added the raised finger — a didactic work not only teaches but insists.

Use the root in a new word: autodidact: Her conference badge listed no university at all - just 'autodidact,' worn like a medal.

Root Check

Word Choice

critical / academic

Didactic judges tone where pedagogical describes craft: a pedagogical choice concerns how teaching works, while calling a work didactic says it pushes its lesson at you — praise in a textbook, a complaint in a film review. Pedagogy, the noun, names the discipline both words orbit.
